moduleTitle: The universe and the place of human beings

note.specFocus: Christian teaching on the origins of the universe and the place and responsibility of human beings within creation.
note.sourcePages: Written to match the Edexcel specification; no supplied booklet for this subject.
note.summary:
1.1 The Universe and the Place of Human Beings
Christians believe the universe was created by God, and that human beings hold a special, responsible place within it.
Two creation accounts in Genesis
Genesis 1: God speaks the universe into being over six days — light, sky, land and plants, sun and moon, sea and sky creatures, land animals, and finally human beings "in our image, after our likeness" — before resting on the seventh day.
Genesis 2: God forms Adam from the dust of the ground and breathes life into him; Eve is later formed from Adam's rib. This account stresses God's personal, hands-on involvement in making humanity.
• Many Christians read these chapters as theological truth about who created the world and why, rather than as a scientific textbook.
• Young Earth creationists read Genesis literally, holding that God created the world in six literal days relatively recently.
• Theistic evolutionists (for example the BioLogos movement) accept the scientific evidence for the Big Bang and evolution, while believing God is the ultimate cause and purpose behind these natural processes.
Imago Dei and stewardship
• Imago Dei ("image of God") is the belief that every human being reflects something of God's nature — reason, creativity, moral responsibility and the capacity to love — giving human life unique value and dignity.
• Genesis 1:28 gives humans "dominion" over the earth and its creatures; most Christians interpret this as a call to responsible stewardship rather than a licence to exploit nature, since the earth remains God's creation, not human property.
• Many Christian environmental movements (e.g. A Rocha, Christian Aid's climate work) appeal to stewardship to argue that caring for creation is a religious duty, not just a practical necessity.
Science and religion
• The cosmological argument (Thomas Aquinas) argues that everything which exists has a cause; since an endless chain of causes is thought impossible, there must be an uncaused first cause, which believers identify as God.
• The Big Bang theory and evolution by natural selection offer scientific explanations of origins; many Christians see these as compatible with, rather than opposed to, belief in a creator God working through natural law.
Exam link: when asked to "choose one religion", use Genesis, imago Dei and stewardship; contrast with non-religious accounts such as the Big Bang and evolution when a question asks for both religious and non-religious views.

questions.modelAnswer:
A strong response develops two separate points:

1. Genesis 1 teaches that God created the universe out of nothing (ex nihilo) in an ordered sequence of six days, speaking light, sky, land, plants, sun and moon, sea creatures, birds, land animals and finally human beings into existence, before resting on the seventh day.

2. Genesis 2 gives a second account in which God forms the first man, Adam, from the dust of the ground and breathes life into him, and later forms Eve from Adam's rib, showing that human life is directly and personally given by God rather than arising by chance.
questions.question: Choose one religion. Outline two teachings about the origins of the universe.

questions.examTip: For a 12-mark evaluation, use accurate religious teaching, explain different religious or non-religious views, analyse the statement and reach a justified conclusion. The conclusion should follow from the arguments you have discussed.
questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE

One line of reasoning is: Genesis opens with the claim that "In the beginning God created the heavens and the earth", so for many Christians the Bible itself is direct testimony that God caused the world to exist.

A second consideration is: The cosmological argument, associated with Thomas Aquinas, reasons that everything which exists has a cause, and that an infinite chain of causes is impossible, so there must be an uncaused first cause which people call God.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE

A different perspective is: Scientific explanations such as the Big Bang theory and evolution by natural selection account for the origin and development of the universe and life through natural processes, without needing to appeal to a creator.

A further consideration is: Non-religious thinkers argue that the existence of unnecessary suffering, and the lack of direct empirical evidence for God, make a divine cause of the world an unproven and unnecessary assumption.

JUDGEMENT

Overall, the conclusion should weigh the arguments above against this key consideration: many Christians, including those who accept scientific accounts such as theistic evolution, would argue the two views are not opposites: God could be the ultimate cause working through the processes that science describes. It should then state which perspective is more convincing in relation to the exact wording of the question and explain why, rather than assuming that every Christian will reach the same view.

questions.modelAnswer:
A FIRST PERSPECTIVE
Teaching gives coherent meaning to the themes of God as creator; stewardship of creation; scientific accounts such as the Big Bang and evolution; differing readings of Genesis and helps Christians decide what is true.

AN ALTERNATIVE PERSPECTIVE
Practice makes belief visible in worship, compassion, family and service; without action faith may be empty. Christians within different traditions may also disagree about how the teaching should be lived.

JUDGEMENT
A reasoned conclusion should compare the authority and practical effect of belief and action, acknowledge diversity, and decide which is more persuasive for the exact claim.
